questions.q: What is the capital of Kazakhstan?
questions.e: It was Astana, then Nur-Sultan, then Astana again. The city has commitment issues.

questions.q: Myanmar moved its capital in the mid-2000s to which purpose-built city?
questions.e: Famous for 20-lane highways with almost no cars. Yangon lost the job.

questions.q: Brazil’s capital Brasília was built from scratch in about how many years?
questions.e: Opened in 1960, shaped roughly like an aeroplane. Rio was not consulted.

questions.q: Bolivia’s constitutional capital is?
questions.e: La Paz runs the government; Sucre keeps the title. Sharing is caring.

questions.q: Sri Lanka’s parliament sits in which capital?
questions.e: Colombo is the commercial capital. Kotte is the one that wins pub quizzes.

questions.q: Officially, Switzerland’s law calls Bern its?
questions.e: Switzerland technically has no capital. Bern just hosts the parliament and the bears.

questions.q: How many capital cities does South Africa have?
questions.e: Pretoria (government), Cape Town (parliament), Bloemfontein (courts). Spread the load.

questions.q: Liberia’s capital, Monrovia, is named after a?
questions.e: James Monroe, the fifth US president. Freed American slaves founded the colony.

questions.q: Kuala Lumpur’s name translates roughly as?
questions.e: Founded where two rivers meet in tin-mining mud. Honest branding.

questions.q: Which is the southernmost capital city of a sovereign country?
questions.e: Windy Welly wins it. Canberra isn’t even close.

questions.q: Who ferried souls across the rivers of the Greek underworld, for a coin?
questions.e: Hermes only walked you to the bank. Charon wanted paying for the trip.

questions.q: Odin’s two ravens are Huginn and Muninn. What do their names mean?
questions.e: They fly the world each day and report back. The original newsfeed.

questions.q: In Norse myth, Ratatoskr is a squirrel who runs up and down the world tree to?
questions.a: Carry insults between an eagle and a dragon
questions.e: A gossiping squirrel stirring up a feud. Mythology predicted comment sections.

questions.q: Which Titan had his liver eaten daily by an eagle for giving fire to humans?
questions.e: Sisyphus got the boulder. Prometheus got the worst breakfast guest ever.

questions.q: Which Titan held up the sky and briefly tricked Heracles into taking a shift?
questions.e: Heracles then tricked him back. Classic workplace handover.

questions.q: In Norse myth, the world will end with a battle called?
questions.e: Valhalla is the hall, Yggdrasil the tree, Bifröst the bridge. Ragnarök is the finale.

questions.q: The Graeae, three sisters of Greek myth, famously shared?
questions.e: They passed them around. Perseus stole the eye. Rude, but effective.

questions.q: In Greek myth, King Midas was given donkey’s ears for?
questions.e: He preferred Pan’s piping to Apollo’s lyre. Apollo did not take feedback well.

questions.q: In Norse myth, which god gave birth to the eight-legged horse Sleipnir?
questions.e: Loki, while disguised as a mare. Norse myth does not do boring.

questions.q: Pandora’s famous ‘box’ was originally a?
questions.e: A 16th-century translation turned the jar into a box. Mistakes were unleashed.

questions.q: What shape is wombat poo?
questions.e: Cubes, so they don’t roll off rocks. Nature’s tidiest toilet.

questions.q: How many hearts does an octopus have?
questions.e: Eight arms, three hearts, blue blood. Overachiever.

questions.q: Why do sea otters hold hands while they sleep?
questions.e: Also wrap themselves in kelp. Adorable and practical.

questions.q: Which bird can fly backwards?
questions.e: Also hovers, and beats its wings up to around 80 times a second. Show-off.

questions.q: A wood frog can survive the winter by?
questions.e: Its heart stops and up to two-thirds of its body water freezes. In spring it thaws and hops off.

questions.q: Where is a shrimp’s heart?
questions.e: Technically the head-and-chest section. Thinking with its heart, literally.

questions.q: How do bottlenose dolphins sleep?
questions.a: Half their brain at a time
questions.e: One half rests while the other keeps watch and remembers to breathe.

questions.q: Which of these animals can’t jump?
questions.e: At least one foot always stays on the ground. Built for stomping, not bouncing.

questions.q: What shape are a goat’s pupils?
questions.e: Helps spot predators across a wide view. And unsettle humans.

questions.q: Cheetahs can’t roar. What do they do instead?
questions.e: A chirping cheetah sounds like a bird. Fastest cat, cutest noises.

questions.q: The OXO Good Grips peeler, with its big soft handle, was inspired by?
questions.e: Sam Farber designed it in 1990 after watching his wife Betsey struggle with a metal peeler.

questions.q: Bendy straws were invented in the 1930s after the inventor watched?
questions.a: His young daughter struggle with a straight straw
questions.e: Hospitals soon used them so patients could drink lying down.

questions.q: An early typewriter, built in Italy around 1808, was made so that?
questions.a: A blind countess could write letters
questions.e: Pellegrino Turri built it for his friend, Countess Carolina Fantoni da Fivizzano.

questions.q: Louis Braille developed his reading system at about what age?
questions.e: He lost his sight after an accident in his father's workshop as a small boy.

questions.q: Braille grew out of?
questions.a: A French army code for reading in the dark
questions.e: Charles Barbier's 'night writing' used raised dots. Braille made it simpler.

questions.q: Zenith's 1950 TV remote, the 'Lazy Bones', was connected to the TV by?
questions.e: People kept tripping over it.

questions.q: When something designed for disabled people ends up helping everyone, like footpath ramps helping prams and suitcases, it's called?
'Talking books' on records were first made in the 1930s for?
questions.a: Blind readers, including blinded war veterans
questions.e: Audiobooks went mainstream decades later.

questions.q: Occupational therapy grew as a profession partly to help people recover from?
questions.e: 'Reconstruction aides' helped wounded soldiers get back to everyday life.

questions.q: Velcro was invented after a Swiss engineer noticed?
questions.a: Burrs stuck in his dog's fur
questions.e: Hook-and-loop fastening now helps anyone who finds buttons and laces fiddly.

questions.q: On Venus, which is longer?
questions.e: It spins so slowly that one day outlasts its year. Also, it spins backwards.

questions.q: Given a big enough bathtub, which planet would float?
questions.e: It’s less dense than water. Good luck finding the bath.

questions.q: Uranus’s upper clouds contain hydrogen sulphide, which smells like?
questions.e: Yes, Uranus smells. The jokes write themselves.

questions.q: What colour are sunsets on Mars?
questions.e: The red planet does blue sunsets. Dust scatters light the opposite way to ours.

questions.q: Astronauts often say space smells like?
questions.e: The smell clings to suits after spacewalks. Barbecue in orbit.

questions.q: A teaspoon of neutron star would weigh roughly?
questions.e: Crushed atoms. Do not attempt to stir your tea with it.

questions.q: Since being discovered in 1930, how many full orbits of the Sun has Pluto completed?
questions.e: One lap takes about 248 years. Its first ‘birthday’ is in 2178.

questions.q: Why will the Apollo astronauts’ footprints last so long?
questions.a: The Moon has no wind or rain
questions.e: They could last millions of years. Littering, but historic.

questions.q: Olympus Mons, the biggest volcano in the solar system, is on?
questions.e: About two and a half times the height of Everest. Io has more volcanoes, but smaller.

questions.q: When you look at the Sun, the light you see left it about how long ago?
questions.e: You’re always looking at the Sun’s past. Slightly spooky.

questions.q: Roughly how many nerve cells are in the human brain?
Your brain is about 2% of your body weight. Roughly how much of your energy does it use?
questions.e: Thinking is hungry work.

questions.q: The proper name for 'brain freeze' from ice-cream is?
questions.e: Warming the roof of your mouth with your tongue helps.

questions.q: The fastest nerve signals travel at about?
questions.e: That's well over 400 km/h.

questions.q: In the stroke warning sign FAST, what does F stand for?
questions.e: Face drooping, Arms can't lift, Speech slurred, Time to call 000.

questions.q: London cabbies who learn 'The Knowledge' were found to have a bigger?
questions.e: A famous 2000 brain-scan study.

questions.q: Why is it so hard to tickle yourself?
questions.a: Your brain predicts the touch and dulls it
w: Your skin is numb to your own fingers

questions.q: How much of your brain do you actually use?
questions.a: Nearly all of it, at different times
questions.e: The 10% idea is a myth. Sorry, Hollywood.

questions.q: If you think someone is having a stroke, what should you do?
w: Give them a big glass of water
Book a GP visit for tomorrow
questions.e: Time is brain: the sooner the treatment, the more brain is saved.

questions.q: The left side of your brain mostly controls?
questions.a: The right side of your body
w: The left side of your body

questions.q: Which invention came after a chocolate bar melted in an engineer’s pocket near radar gear?
questions.e: Percy Spencer, 1945. Snacks have been reheated unevenly ever since.

questions.q: Bubble wrap was first invented as?
questions.e: Textured wallpaper, 1957. Nobody wanted it on walls; everyone wanted to pop it.

questions.q: Post-it Notes came from a glue that was?
questions.e: A failed super-glue that turned into a stationery cupboard staple.

questions.q: Velcro was inspired by?
questions.a: Burrs stuck to a dog’s fur
questions.e: George de Mestral went for a walk and came back with an idea and a very clingy dog.

questions.q: The ice pop (ice lolly) on a stick was supposedly invented in 1905 by a?
questions.e: Frank Epperson left his drink outside overnight with the stirrer in. Genius by neglect.

questions.q: Play-Doh was originally sold as?
questions.e: Coal heating went out of fashion, so it was rebranded as a toy.

questions.q: The Slinky was invented by a naval engineer who?
questions.a: Knocked a spring off a shelf
questions.e: It ‘walked’ instead of falling. Ships’ loss, kids’ gain.

questions.q: Super glue was first rejected because, while making clear plastic gun sights, it?
questions.e: Harry Coover’s team found it too sticky. Years later, that was the point.

questions.q: Which sweetener was discovered when a chemist didn’t wash his hands before dinner?
questions.e: 1879. His bread tasted sweet. Hygiene: optional, apparently.

questions.q: In 1965, chemist Stephanie Kwolek refused to bin a cloudy, runny solution her colleagues doubted. It became?
questions.e: Pound for pound about five times stronger than steel. It’s in bulletproof vests.

questions.q: Halloween has roots in which Celtic festival?
questions.e: Beltane is the May one. Samhain marked summer’s end and spooky season.

questions.q: In Ireland and Scotland, jack-o’-lanterns were originally carved from?
questions.e: Pumpkins won in America because they’re easier to carve. Turnip faces are terrifying.

questions.q: How many times did Dracula author Bram Stoker visit Transylvania?
questions.e: He researched it from libraries. Imagination is cheaper than flights.

questions.q: In Mary Shelley’s novel, the monster’s creator is called?
questions.e: Frankenstein is the doctor, not the monster. And Igor isn’t in the book at all.

questions.q: Mary Shelley wrote Frankenstein during a gloomy ‘year without a summer’ caused by?
questions.e: Mount Tambora erupted in 1815. Bad weather, great horror.

questions.q: In Scotland, children dressing up and performing for treats is traditionally called?
questions.e: You had to earn the sweets with a joke or song. No freeloading.

questions.q: Vlad the Impaler, Dracula’s inspiration, ruled which region?
questions.e: Transylvania gets the castle tourism. Wallachia got the actual Vlad.

questions.q: Which famous escape artist died on Halloween in 1926?
questions.e: A spooky date for the man who escaped everything else.

questions.q: Candy corn was originally marketed under which name?
questions.e: Corn was mostly animal feed back then. Delicious branding.

questions.q: Which Michael Jackson track features a creepy voice-over by Vincent Price?
questions.e: ‘Ghosts’ was a good guess, but Thriller had the cackle.

questions.q: ‘Salary’ comes from a Latin word linked to?
questions.e: The ‘paid in salt’ legend is shakier than the word itself.

questions.q: The ¶ symbol is called a?
questions.e: The obelus is the ÷ sign. The pilcrow marks paragraphs and pub-quiz smugness.

questions.q: The word ‘robot’ comes from a Czech word meaning?
questions.e: Coined in Karel Čapek’s 1920 play. Bleak origins for a vacuum cleaner.

questions.q: ‘Disaster’ literally means?
questions.e: Blame the astrologers.

questions.q: The word ‘nice’ originally meant?
questions.e: From Latin ‘nescius’, ignorant. Calling someone nice used to be an insult.

questions.q: ‘Shampoo’ entered English from which language?
questions.e: From ‘champo’, to press or massage. The French did not invent everything fancy.

questions.q: ‘Avocado’ comes from an Aztec (Nahuatl) word that also meant?
questions.e: Look at a pair hanging on a tree. You’ll see it now. Sorry.

questions.q: A ‘clue’ was originally a?
questions.e: Theseus followed one out of the labyrinth. Solving mysteries ever since.

questions.q: ‘Sesquipedalian’ describes?
questions.e: Literally ‘a foot and a half long’. Fittingly, it is one.

questions.q: A misheard song lyric is called a?
questions.e: From ‘laid him on the green’ heard as ‘Lady Mondegreen’. Everyone sings them wrong.

questions.q: Which country has the only non-rectangular national flag?
questions.e: Two stacked triangles. Rectangles are for the unadventurous.

questions.q: Which country’s flag is square?
questions.e: Vatican City is square too. Everyone else stuck with rectangles.

questions.q: Which country’s flag features an AK-47 rifle?
questions.e: Crossed with a hoe and a book. Unique, to say the least.

questions.q: Which country’s flag features a dragon?
questions.e: The ‘Land of the Thunder Dragon’. China has loads of dragons, just not on its flag.

questions.q: Which country’s flag has a different design on each side?
questions.e: Different emblems front and back. Double the printing, double the fun.

questions.q: Which country’s flag is widely recognised as the oldest still in use?
questions.e: The Dannebrog. Legend says it fell from the sky in 1219.

questions.q: From 1977 to 2011, which country’s flag was plain green, with nothing else on it?
questions.e: Easiest flag ever to draw. Now it has stripes and a crescent.

questions.q: Which country’s flag shows a map of the country itself?
questions.e: Copper-coloured island on white. Hard to get lost.

questions.q: The flags of Indonesia and Monaco are?
questions.e: Red over white. Only the proportions differ. Awkward.

questions.q: On the Aboriginal flag, designed by Luritja artist Harold Thomas in 1971, the yellow circle represents?
questions.e: Black for Aboriginal people, red for the earth and the spiritual relationship to the land, yellow for the Sun, the giver of life.

questions.q: Which horse did the Roman emperor Caligula supposedly plan to make a consul?
questions.e: Incitatus reportedly had a marble stall and an ivory manger. The consulship may have been a joke. May.

questions.q: Bucephalus was the famous warhorse of?
questions.e: Alexander tamed him as a boy by turning him to face the sun, so he couldn't see his own shadow.

questions.q: Laika, the first animal to orbit the Earth, was a?
questions.e: A stray from the streets of Moscow, launched on Sputnik 2 in 1957.

questions.q: Dolly, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell, was a?
questions.e: Born in Scotland in 1996, cloned from a mammary cell and named after Dolly Parton.

questions.q: Hachikō, the dog who waited at a Tokyo station for years after his owner died, was which breed?
questions.e: He waited at Shibuya station for almost ten years. He now has a statue there.

questions.q: Paul the Octopus became famous in 2010 for?
questions.e: He picked from two food boxes marked with flags. He got all eight of his 2010 predictions right.

questions.q: Ham, the first great ape launched into space in 1961, was a?
questions.e: He pulled levers on cue during the flight and came home safely.

questions.q: Secretariat is famous for winning the 1973 Belmont Stakes by about?
questions.e: It sealed the US Triple Crown. His record time still stands.

questions.q: What kind of animal was Knut, a celebrity at Berlin Zoo?
questions.e: Hand-raised by a keeper after his mother rejected him. Merchandise followed.

questions.q: Cher Ami, a hero of the First World War, was a?
questions.e: Shot through the breast, he still delivered a message that saved nearly 200 American soldiers.

questions.q: In the original book, Dorothy’s magic slippers are?
questions.e: The film made them ruby to show off Technicolor. Glass is Cinderella.

questions.q: The crew nicknamed the mechanical shark in Jaws?
questions.e: Reportedly after Spielberg’s lawyer. It kept breaking, so you barely see it.

questions.q: The blood in Psycho’s famous shower scene was actually?
questions.e: In black and white, syrup looked better. Hitchcock knew his sauces.

questions.q: The ‘Wilhelm scream’ is famous for being?
questions.a: A sound effect reused in hundreds of films
questions.e: Star Wars, Indiana Jones, Toy Story. Same scream, many unlucky extras.

questions.q: In Citizen Kane, ‘Rosebud’ turns out to be a?
questions.e: Spoiler, from 1941. You’ve had time.

questions.q: Mad Max: Fury Road was mainly filmed in?
questions.e: Outback Broken Hill turned green after rain. An Aussie franchise, exported to Africa.

questions.q: The lightsaber hum in Star Wars was created from?
questions.a: An old projector motor and TV interference
questions.e: Sound designer Ben Burtt, mixing junk into magic.

questions.q: Which actor played James Bond in just one official film, On Her Majesty’s Secret Service?
questions.e: He was a model with almost no acting experience. Turned down a seven-film deal.

questions.q: Some velociraptor noises in Jurassic Park came from recordings of?
questions.e: Terrifying on screen. Much less so in context.

questions.q: During World War II, Oscar statuettes were made of?
questions.e: Metal was rationed. Winners swapped them for metal ones after the war.

questions.q: Which country covers the most time zones, counting territories?
questions.e: Thanks to islands everywhere. China, huge as it is, uses just one.

questions.q: Which country has the most natural lakes?
questions.e: Finland is ‘the land of a thousand lakes’. Canada has way more.

questions.q: What is the world’s largest desert?
questions.e: Deserts are about dryness, not heat. The Sahara gets bronze-level sulking.

questions.q: At their closest, Russia and the USA are about how far apart?
questions.e: Two Diomede islands in the Bering Strait. Also almost a day apart in time.

questions.q: Point Nemo, the most remote spot in the ocean, is used as a?
questions.e: Dead satellites get crashed there. The nearest humans are often astronauts.

questions.q: Which mountain’s summit is the farthest point from Earth’s centre?
questions.e: Earth bulges at the equator, giving this Ecuadorian peak the edge. Everest is taller from sea level.

questions.q: Which major river crosses the Equator twice?
questions.e: It loops north and then back south of the line on its way to the Atlantic.

questions.q: Which is wider: Australia or the Moon?
questions.e: Australia is about 4000 km wide. The Moon is about 3500 km across.

questions.q: Which country is completely surrounded by South Africa?
questions.e: Eswatini also borders Mozambique. Lesotho is fully hugged.

questions.q: What is the world’s smallest country?
questions.e: Smaller than many golf courses. Monaco is a distant second.

questions.q: Banksy’s Girl with Balloon shredded itself at auction. What happened next?
questions.e: Renamed Love is in the Bin and resold for millions more.

questions.q: The pigment ultramarine was originally made from?
questions.e: Ground-up gemstone, once pricier than gold. Painters used it sparingly.

questions.q: When the Mona Lisa was stolen in 1911, which artist was questioned by police?
questions.e: He was cleared. The thief was a museum handyman who hid it under his coat.

questions.q: Michelangelo’s David was originally meant to stand?
questions.e: Too heavy to lift up there. Lucky for our necks.

questions.q: ‘Mummy brown’, a pigment used by painters, was made from?
questions.e: Really. Some artists buried their tubes once they found out.

questions.q: Between 1912 and 1948, the Olympics awarded medals for?
questions.e: Painting, sculpture, music and literature. Very sporty.

questions.q: Marcel Duchamp’s famous 1917 artwork ‘Fountain’ is a?
questions.e: Signed ‘R. Mutt’. Art history was never the same.

questions.q: Maurizio Cattelan’s artwork ‘Comedian’, sold for millions, is?
questions.a: A banana taped to a wall
questions.e: The 2024 buyer then ate the banana. The tape survived.

questions.q: Which painter cut off part of his own ear in 1888?
questions.e: It happened after an argument with Gauguin in Arles. He later painted a self-portrait with the bandage.

questions.q: After a bus crash left her in pain for life, which artist began painting self-portraits from her bed?
questions.e: Her mother had a special easel made and a mirror fitted above the bed. More than a third of her paintings are self-portraits.

questions.q: The microwave oven was invented after a radar engineer noticed?
questions.a: A chocolate bar melted in his pocket
questions.e: Percy Spencer, 1945. Popcorn was one of the first things he tried.

questions.q: Which everyday fruit is very slightly radioactive?
questions.e: Thanks to potassium. You'd need to eat millions at once to worry.

questions.q: Many home smoke alarms contain a tiny amount of?
questions.e: It helps the alarm sense smoke particles. The amount is very small and sealed in.

questions.q: The 'Radium Girls' of the 1920s were?
questions.a: Factory workers poisoned by glowing watch paint
questions.e: They were told to lick their brushes to a point. Their court cases changed workplace safety.

questions.q: An MRI scanner's magnet is so strong it can?
questions.a: Pull metal objects like oxygen cylinders across the room
questions.e: That's why everyone gets checked for metal first.

questions.q: Why do MRI scanners bang and buzz so loudly?
questions.a: Coils inside vibrate as the magnetic field switches
w: It's a recording to keep you awake

questions.q: Medical ultrasound uses sound that is?
questions.a: Too high-pitched for humans to hear
w: Too low for humans to hear
As loud as a rock concert

questions.q: Which animal 'sees' with sound, using the same physics as ultrasound?
questions.e: Dolphins do it too.

questions.q: Glow-in-the-dark ceiling stars work by?
questions.a: Storing light and releasing it slowly
questions.e: Old watch dials really did use radium. Modern stars don't.

questions.q: The unit of magnetic field strength used for MRI scanners is named after?
questions.e: Most hospital scanners are 1.5 or 3 tesla.

questions.q: Wilhelm Röntgen called his discovery 'X' rays because?
The first famous X-ray image, made in 1895, shows?
questions.a: His wife's hand and wedding ring

questions.q: On seeing her bones, Röntgen's wife Anna Bertha reportedly said?
From the 1920s to the 1950s, many shoe shops used X-ray machines to?
questions.e: Customers watched their toe bones wiggle. Not a great idea, it turned out.

questions.q: Röntgen refused to patent X-rays and gave his Nobel prize money to?
questions.e: He wanted everyone to benefit.

questions.q: How soon after Röntgen's 1895 announcement were X-rays used on patients?
Marie Curie's mobile X-ray vans in World War I were nicknamed?
questions.e: 'Petites Curies'. She drove some herself.

questions.q: Marie Curie's daughter Irène also won a Nobel Prize, in?
questions.e: In 1935, with her husband Frédéric Joliot.

questions.q: Marie Curie's coffin in Paris is lined with lead because?
questions.a: Her body was thought to be radioactive

questions.q: The first CT scanner was built at EMI, the company that also signed?
questions.e: Godfrey Hounsfield shared a Nobel Prize for it in 1979.

questions.q: Why was Canberra built as the capital?
questions.e: A compromise city, built between the two bickering siblings.

questions.q: The Dingo Fence is roughly how long?
questions.e: One of the longest fences on Earth. The dingoes are unimpressed.

questions.q: Australia has the world’s largest wild population of?
questions.e: Brought in for outback transport, then released. Now there are a lot.

questions.q: The Great Barrier Reef, the world’s biggest reef system, was built by?
questions.e: Billions of tiny animals, building limestone skeletons for thousands of years. Big enough to see from space.

questions.q: Kangaroos find it almost impossible to?
questions.e: It’s partly why the kangaroo and emu are on Australia’s coat of arms: both are said to only go forward.

questions.q: Vegemite is made mainly from?
questions.e: A by-product of beer. Spread thinly, or regret it.

questions.q: Male lyrebirds are famous for mimicking?
questions.e: They copy other birds too, sometimes 20 species in a single song.

questions.q: Roughly how many tiles cover the Sydney Opera House roof?
questions.e: 1,056,006 of them, made in Sweden. Self-cleaning, too.

questions.q: The Trans-Australian Railway across the Nullarbor has the world’s longest straight stretch, about?
questions.e: Not a single curve. Drivers stay awake somehow.

questions.q: Climbing Uluru was banned in 2019, out of respect for its Traditional Owners, the?
questions.e: Uluru, in the Northern Territory, is sacred to the Anangu. It was handed back to them in 1985.

questions.q: What is the name of Jon Snow’s direwolf in Game of Thrones?
questions.e: The white runt of the litter. Fans felt he deserved more screen time and at least one hug.

questions.q: Which Simpsons catchphrase made it into the Oxford English Dictionary?
questions.e: Added in 2001. Homer, lexicographer.

questions.q: What breed of dog is Bluey?
questions.e: An Australian Cattle Dog. Her dad Bandit is one too.

questions.q: Squid Game comes from which country?
questions.e: Netflix’s most-watched series ever. The creator spent ten years trying to get it made.

questions.q: What is the coffee shop in Friends called?
questions.e: MacLaren’s is a bar from How I Met Your Mother. Different couch.

questions.q: What is Doctor Who’s time machine called?
questions.e: Time And Relative Dimension In Space. Bigger on the inside.

questions.q: The first official TV advert, in the US in 1941, was for?
questions.e: A Bulova clock face for about ten seconds. Advertising has grown louder since.

questions.q: In Breaking Bad, what alias does Walter White use?
questions.e: Named after a physicist. Chemistry teachers, take note.

questions.q: Stranger Things is set in which fictional town?
questions.e: Home of the Upside Down, a suspicious lab and an excellent arcade.

questions.q: David Brent is the boss in which show?
questions.e: Before America got Michael Scott, Slough had David Brent.

questions.q: The armistice ending fighting in World War I took effect at 11am on 11 November of which year?
questions.e: The eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month.

questions.q: The red poppy as a symbol of remembrance was inspired by which poem?
questions.e: Written by Canadian John McCrae in 1915.

questions.q: Why did poppies bloom across the Western Front battlefields?
w: They grow best in cold weather
questions.e: Churned earth let dormant seeds sprout. A striking sight among the devastation.

questions.q: The Ode recited at Remembrance services comes from which poem?
questions.e: By Laurence Binyon: ‘They shall grow not old, as we that are left grow old.’

questions.q: In the UK, how long is the silence traditionally kept at 11am on Armistice Day?
questions.e: Many countries keep one minute; Britain has kept two since 1919.

questions.q: The Tomb of the Unknown Warrior, opened in 1920, is in which London building?
questions.e: It’s the only tomb in the Abbey that nobody walks on.

questions.q: The Gallipoli peninsula is in which modern country?
questions.e: Allied troops landed there on 25 April 1915, now marked as Anzac Day.

questions.q: The Last Post is traditionally played on which instrument?
questions.e: Once a camp signal marking the end of the day, it now farewells the fallen.

questions.q: Edith Cavell, executed in 1915 for helping Allied soldiers escape occupied Belgium, was a British?
questions.e: She treated wounded soldiers from both sides. ‘Patriotism is not enough’ are among her last recorded words.

questions.q: On Christmas Day 1914, many British and German soldiers famously?
questions.e: They sang carols, swapped gifts and, by some accounts, played football in no man’s land.

questions.q: The cloud from a big sneeze can carry droplets up to about?
questions.e: Catch it in your elbow.

questions.q: Is it impossible to sneeze with your eyes open?
questions.a: No, it's a strong reflex, but it can be done
w: Yes, your eyes would pop out

questions.q: 'Influenza' comes from the Italian for?
questions.e: People once blamed it on the influence of the stars.

questions.q: In 1854 John Snow traced a cholera outbreak in London to?
questions.e: Removing the pump handle helped end it.

questions.q: The word 'malaria' comes from Italian for?
questions.e: Before germ theory, smells got the blame.

questions.q: Which nurse used colourful charts to show more soldiers were dying of disease than of wounds?
In the 1840s, who showed that doctors washing their hands saved mothers' lives?
questions.e: Many colleagues ignored him at the time.

questions.q: Washing your hands properly takes about as long as?
w: A full song on the radio
questions.e: About 20 seconds.

questions.q: The medical word for a sneeze is?
questions.e: Eructation is a burp. Singultus is a hiccup.

questions.q: Which vaccine protects against the most common bacterial cause of pneumonia?
questions.e: Worth asking about if you're older or have a long-term health condition.

questions.q: Fear of the number 13 is called?
questions.e: Fear of Friday the 13th has its own word too: paraskevidekatriaphobia. Happy Friday.

questions.q: Breaking a mirror supposedly brings how many years of bad luck?
questions.e: Seven years, plus the cost of a new mirror.

questions.q: In Japan and China, which number is unlucky because it sounds like ‘death’?
questions.e: Some buildings skip the 4th floor entirely. Eight is the lucky one.

questions.q: In Italy, which number is traditionally unlucky?
questions.e: XVII rearranges to VIXI, Latin for ‘I have lived’. Ominous.

questions.q: In Spain and much of Latin America, the unlucky day is?
questions.e: Today would be fine there. Tuesday is when they hide.

questions.q: Which number is famously lucky in Chinese culture because it sounds like ‘prosper’?
questions.e: The Beijing Olympics opened at 8pm on 8/8/08. No coincidence.

questions.q: In Britain and Australia, ‘knock on wood’ is usually said as?
questions.e: Same idea. Less knocking, more touching.

questions.q: Spilt salt is traditionally thrown over which shoulder?
questions.e: Supposedly into the eye of the devil lurking there. Rude, but effective.

questions.q: Which Shakespeare play’s name is considered unlucky to say inside a theatre?
questions.e: Actors call it ‘the Scottish play’. Say it, and you may be sent outside to spin.

questions.q: What do actors traditionally say instead of ‘good luck’?
questions.e: Wishing good luck is considered, ironically, bad luck.

questions.q: Doctors in ancient India noticed that the urine of people with diabetes attracted?
questions.e: Because it was sweet.

questions.q: 'Mellitus', as in diabetes mellitus, means?
questions.e: 'Diabetes' means 'passing through', for all the urine.

questions.q: In January 1922 the first person to be given insulin, Leonard Thompson, was how old?
questions.e: He lived another 13 years.

questions.q: Before the 1980s, most insulin came from?
In 1978 human insulin became one of the first medicines made using?
questions.e: It reached patients in 1982.

questions.q: A type 2 diabetes medicine was developed from the saliva of which animal?
questions.e: The drug is exenatide.

questions.q: What colour is the circle in the World Diabetes Day logo?
Sugar cane was first farmed thousands of years ago in?
The sweetener saccharin was discovered in 1879 when a chemist?
questions.a: Forgot to wash his hands before dinner
questions.e: His bread tasted strangely sweet.

questions.q: Specially trained dogs can alert their owners to?
questions.e: They're thought to pick up a change in breath scent.

questions.q: What is the world’s second-largest island?
questions.e: After Greenland. Borneo is third.

questions.q: Easter Island’s famous moai statues are often more than heads. They have?
questions.e: Many have whole torsos underground. They’re not just heads, they’re buried statues.

questions.q: Which island is famous for umbrella-shaped dragon’s blood trees?
questions.e: Off Yemen. Looks like another planet.

questions.q: Every year, tens of millions of red crabs migrate across which Australian island?
questions.e: Roads close for crab traffic. Locals sweep them along.

questions.q: Napoleon died in exile on which island?
questions.e: He escaped Elba. Saint Helena was far enough to stop that nonsense.

questions.q: Canada and Denmark had a decades-long ‘Whisky War’ over Hans Island, ended in 2022 by?
questions.e: They used to leave bottles of whisky and schnapps for each other. Very polite war.

questions.q: Japan’s Ōkunoshima is famous for being overrun with?
questions.e: Cat Island and deer-filled Nara exist too. This one’s the bunny one.

questions.q: Brazil’s Ilha da Queimada Grande is closed to the public because it’s full of?
questions.e: Snake Island. Visitors need special permission and nerves.

questions.q: Lemurs live in the wild only on which island?
questions.e: About 90% of Madagascar’s wildlife is found nowhere else on Earth.

questions.q: According to the sagas, why did Erik the Red name Greenland ‘Greenland’?
questions.e: Arguably history’s first real estate marketing. Most of it is ice.

questions.q: The marathon is 42.195 km because of?
w: The length of a Roman road
questions.e: The course was set to finish in front of the royal box. The extra bit stuck.

questions.q: In 1973, Billie Jean King beat Bobby Riggs in a tennis match nicknamed?
questions.e: Tens of millions watched on TV. She won in straight sets.

questions.q: What did astronaut Alan Shepard do on the Moon in 1971?
questions.e: One-handed, in a spacesuit. Still the most out-of-bounds shot ever.

questions.q: Which of these was once an Olympic sport?
questions.e: Contested from 1900 to 1920. Britain did quite well.

questions.q: Olympic gold medals are mostly made of?
questions.e: Just a gold coating. The last solid gold ones were in 1912.

questions.q: Wimbledon uses what to scare off pigeons?
questions.e: His name is Rufus. He has his own fans.

questions.q: When the World Cup trophy was stolen in 1966, who found it?
questions.e: Wrapped in newspaper under a hedge. Pickles was a national hero.

questions.q: Basketball was first played with?
questions.e: Someone had to climb up to get the ball out after every basket.

questions.q: The longest tennis match ever, at Wimbledon in 2010, lasted about?
questions.e: The final set ended 70–68. The scoreboard broke.

questions.q: The Paralympic movement grew out of games for injured Second World War veterans held in 1948 at which English hospital?
questions.e: Organised by neurologist Ludwig Guttmann. The first Paralympic Games followed in Rome in 1960.

questions.q: About how many babies worldwide are born premature?
questions.e: Today is World Prematurity Day.

questions.q: A baby counts as premature if born before?
Babies are born with roughly how many bones?
questions.e: Many fuse as they grow. Adults have 206.

questions.q: For the first few weeks, newborns usually cry without?
questions.e: Tear glands are still getting going.

questions.q: Newborns see most clearly at about?
questions.a: 20 to 30 cm, about the distance to a parent's face

questions.q: A newborn's stomach on day one is about the size of?
Babies are born able to?
questions.e: The grasp reflex.

questions.q: The Apgar score that checks every newborn is named after?
questions.e: An anaesthetist who designed it in 1952.

questions.q: In the early 1900s, premature babies in incubators were shown to the public at?
questions.e: Entry fees paid for their care, and many survived.

questions.q: A newborn's first poo, dark green and sticky, is called?
questions.e: Colostrum is early milk; lanugo is fine body hair; vernix is the waxy coating.

questions.q: The Guinness record for holding your breath under water (after breathing pure oxygen) is?
questions.e: Please don't try this at home.

questions.q: Which lung is smaller, to make room for the heart?
Roughly how many breaths does an adult take each day?
Hiccups are spasms of the?
Bar-headed geese can fly over?
questions.e: Where each breath holds about a third of the oxygen at sea level.

questions.q: In 1978, who first climbed Everest without bottled oxygen?
questions.e: Hillary and Tenzing used oxygen in 1953.

questions.q: Which animals manage with no lungs at all?
questions.e: They breathe through their skin.

questions.q: The world's first long-term successful single lung transplant was done in 1983 in?
Opened out, the air sacs in your lungs have a surface area roughly the size of?
questions.e: Somewhere around 50 to 75 square metres.

questions.q: Penicillin was discovered in 1928 when Alexander Fleming came back from holiday to find?
questions.a: Mould killing bacteria on a dish
w: A new insect in his desk
questions.e: Today also starts World AMR Awareness Week: use antibiotics only when needed.

questions.q: Selling chewing gum has been banned since 1992 in?
questions.e: Mostly to stop gum gumming up the trains.

questions.q: In Switzerland, it’s illegal to keep just one of which pet?
questions.e: They’re social, so they need a friend. You can even rent one.

questions.q: In Germany, it’s an offence to run out of fuel on the?
questions.e: Stopping unnecessarily on the Autobahn is banned, and that includes running dry.

questions.q: Since 2009, which footwear is banned at Greece’s ancient sites?
questions.e: They damage the ancient stone. Sensible shoes for the Acropolis.

questions.q: Since 2019, you can be fined for sitting on which Rome landmark?
questions.e: Steps are for walking, apparently. Gelato elsewhere.

questions.q: In Denmark, new babies’ names must generally come from?
questions.e: Anything off the list needs official approval. Creative spelling is not welcome.

questions.q: Under the UK Salmon Act 1986, it’s an offence to handle salmon?
questions.e: It’s about poached fish. Still the funniest phrase in British law.

questions.q: Which ‘weird British law’ is actually a myth?
w: Flying a kite in London streets
questions.e: The others are real. Dying anywhere is not a crime, thankfully.

questions.q: Which country banned strong beer until 1989?
questions.e: Beer Day on 1 March celebrates the end of it. Skál.

questions.q: An 1839 law makes it an offence to fly a kite to the annoyance of others in?
questions.e: The Metropolitan Police Act. Annoying kite flyers, you’ve been warned.

questions.q: In summer heat, the Eiffel Tower?
questions.a: Grows up to about 15 cm taller
questions.e: The iron expands. It was also meant to be temporary.

questions.q: The Sydney Opera House’s designer, Jørn Utzon, saw the finished building?
questions.e: He quit mid-build in 1966 and never returned to see it.

questions.q: The Leaning Tower of Pisa was built as a?
questions.e: Started leaning while still being built. Soft soil, firm commitment.

questions.q: What is the official colour of San Francisco’s Golden Gate Bridge?
questions.e: Not golden at all. The name comes from the strait it spans.

questions.q: When it was new, the Statue of Liberty was what colour?
questions.e: Copper turns green over time. She went full patina within a few decades.

questions.q: Strictly speaking, ‘Big Ben’ is the name of the?
questions.e: The tower is the Elizabeth Tower. Ben just does the bonging.

questions.q: Behind Mount Rushmore’s heads there is a?
questions.e: The Hall of Records. It holds panels explaining the monument.

questions.q: The Taj Mahal was built as a?
questions.e: Shah Jahan built it for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631. It took about 20 years.

questions.q: Barcelona’s Sagrada Família has been under construction since?
questions.e: Gaudí reportedly said his client was not in a hurry.

questions.q: Can you see the Great Wall of China from space with the naked eye?
questions.e: Too narrow and the same colour as the land. Astronauts have checked.

questions.q: In a group of clownfish, what happens when the dominant female dies?
questions.e: Finding Nemo quietly skipped that part.

questions.q: Which sea creature has blue blood?
questions.e: Copper-based blood. Royal, technically.

questions.q: What is the largest fish in the world?
questions.e: Up to about 18 metres, and it eats plankton. Gentle giant.

questions.q: Which seahorse parent gives birth?
w: Neither, they lay eggs on coral
questions.e: The female deposits eggs in his pouch. He does the rest.

questions.q: Which jellyfish is nicknamed ‘immortal’?
questions.e: It can revert to its youthful polyp stage. Envious, aren’t we?

questions.q: Which of the major oceans is the saltiest?
questions.e: The Arctic is the least salty. Melting ice dilutes it.

questions.q: A narwhal’s tusk is actually a?
questions.e: An overgrown tooth that can reach three metres. Ultimate snaggletooth.

questions.q: Which mammal holds the record for the deepest dive?
questions.e: Nearly 3 km down. The sperm whale is impressive, but second.

questions.q: Which sea has no coastline?
questions.e: Bounded by ocean currents, not land. The Dead Sea is really a lake.

questions.q: Roughly what share of Earth’s surface is ocean?
questions.e: Planet Earth is mostly Planet Water.

questions.q: After Haydn was buried, what happened to his skull?
questions.a: It was stolen, and reunited in 1954
w: It was put on display in his piano
It was sent to Mozart’s family
questions.e: Phrenology fans nicked it. Head and body were apart for about 145 years.

questions.q: Mozart kept a pet starling that could sing part of?
questions.e: It sang it with its own wrong notes. Mozart wrote them down anyway.

questions.q: Tchaikovsky’s 1812 Overture famously calls for?
questions.e: Bells too. Orchestra managers dread it.

questions.q: Erik Satie’s piano piece ‘Vexations’ is meant to be repeated how many times?
questions.e: A full performance can take well over 12 hours. Bring snacks.

questions.q: Ravel’s Boléro is built on one long?
questions.e: Same tune for about 15 minutes, just louder and louder.

questions.q: Stravinsky’s The Rite of Spring caused near-riots at its 1913 premiere in?
questions.e: Audiences booed, fought and threw things. Tough crowd.

questions.q: Haydn’s ‘Surprise’ Symphony got its name from?
questions.e: A quiet tune, then BANG. Waking dozing audiences since 1792.

questions.q: Which 12th-century German abbess is one of the earliest composers we know by name?
questions.e: She also wrote about medicine and plants, and corresponded with popes and emperors.

questions.q: Queen Victoria told Felix Mendelssohn her favourite of his songs was ‘Italien’. Who had actually written it?
questions.e: Some of Fanny Mendelssohn’s songs were published under Felix’s name. He owned up on the spot.

questions.q: ‘A cappella’ literally means?
questions.a: In the manner of the chapel
questions.e: Singing with no instruments. Pitch Perfect didn’t invent it.

questions.q: The world’s shortest scheduled flight, between two Orkney islands, takes about?
questions.e: Westray to Papa Westray. With a tailwind it’s under a minute. Don’t bother with the movie.

questions.q: In 1967 Sweden switched from driving on the left to the right?
questions.e: ‘Dagen H’. Everyone stopped, swapped sides, and carried on.

questions.q: The first speeding ticket, in England in 1896, was for going about?
questions.e: About 8 mph in a 2 mph zone. Reckless.

questions.q: Which of these countries drives on the left?
questions.e: So do the UK, India, Australia and about 70 other countries and territories.

questions.q: Melbourne has the world’s largest urban network of?
questions.e: Hook turns included at no extra charge.

questions.q: In Venice, a ‘vaporetto’ is a?
questions.e: Gondolas are for tourists and proposals. Locals catch the vaporetto.

questions.q: Concorde could fly from London to New York in about?
questions.e: Faster than the Earth spins, so you’d land ‘before’ you left, local time.

questions.q: London’s Underground is nicknamed?
questions.e: Opened in 1863, it’s the oldest underground railway in the world.

questions.q: The Trans-Siberian Railway runs from Moscow to?
questions.e: About 9,300 km and seven time zones. Bring snacks.

questions.q: What is Japan’s high-speed bullet train called?
questions.e: Delays are measured in seconds. The TGV is French.

questions.q: In the Atlantic, a tropical cyclone is called a?
questions.e: Typhoon is the north-west Pacific name. Same storm, different postcode.

questions.q: To see a rainbow, where should the sun be?
questions.e: Facing the sun gets you nothing but squinting.

questions.q: A lightning bolt can be roughly how hot compared to the Sun’s surface?
questions.e: Around 30,000°C. The Sun’s surface is a mere 5500°C.

questions.q: A ‘haboob’ is a?
questions.e: A wall of dust that can be over a kilometre tall. Common in Sudan and Arizona.

questions.q: Fog is basically?
questions.e: So walking through fog is walking through a cloud. Fancy.

questions.q: Counting from lightning flash to thunder, about how many seconds equal one kilometre?
questions.e: Five seconds is roughly a mile. Different units, same rumble.

questions.q: When it ‘rains fish’, the likely cause is?
questions.e: It’s been reported in outback Australia too. Bring an umbrella and a pan.

questions.q: The hottest air temperature officially recorded on Earth, 56.7°C, was in?
questions.e: Back in 1913. Some experts doubt the reading, but it still stands as the official record.

questions.q: Thunder and lightning during a snowstorm is called?
questions.e: Rare and very dramatic. Weather nerds lose their minds.

questions.q: The ‘Morning Glory’, a giant tube-shaped cloud, is famous near which Australian town?
questions.e: Glider pilots surf it. Seriously.

questions.q: Before he was Mario, Nintendo’s hero was called?
questions.e: In Donkey Kong, 1981. Then named after a landlord, the story goes.

questions.q: In his first game, Mario’s job was?
questions.e: The plumbing came later. Career pivot.

questions.q: Pac-Man’s creator said the shape was inspired by?
questions.a: A pizza with a slice missing
questions.e: Hungry design, hungry character.

questions.q: Tetris was created in which country?
questions.e: By Alexey Pajitnov in 1984. Falling blocks, from behind the Iron Curtain.

questions.q: What is the best-selling video game of all time?
questions.e: Over 300 million copies of block-placing joy.

questions.q: In The Legend of Zelda, what is the hero’s name?
questions.e: Zelda is the princess. Calling him Zelda is gaming’s oldest mistake.

questions.q: ‘Up, up, down, down, left, right, left, right, B, A’ is the famous?
questions.e: Originally to make a game easier. Now hidden in websites everywhere.

questions.q: Pikachu’s name comes from Japanese sounds for?
questions.e: ‘Pika’ is a sparkle, ‘chu’ a mouse squeak. Adorable onomatopoeia.

questions.q: Sonic the Hedgehog is blue because?
w: Blue hedgehogs are common in Japan
questions.e: Sega wanted a mascot to rival Mario. The shoes were inspired by Michael Jackson.

questions.q: Which 1972 game was the first big arcade hit?
questions.e: Two paddles, one dot. The first machine broke because it was stuffed with coins.

questions.q: Australia was the first country to issue banknotes made of?
questions.e: 1988. Survives the washing machine, unlike your receipts.

questions.q: In 2010, a man paid 10,000 bitcoin for?
questions.e: Worth hundreds of millions of dollars or more today. Expensive dinner.

questions.q: On the island of Yap, traditional money includes?
questions.e: Some are taller than a person. Ownership changes without moving them.

questions.q: Which country is credited with the world’s first paper money?
questions.e: Used during the Tang and Song dynasties, about 1,000 years ago.

questions.q: Why do some coins have ridged edges?
questions.a: To stop people shaving off metal
questions.e: When coins held real silver, clippers trimmed the edges. Ridges exposed them.

questions.q: The word ‘dollar’ comes from a silver coin minted in?
questions.e: The ‘thaler’, from Joachimsthal. Now in the Czech Republic.

questions.q: Euro notes and coins went into circulation in which year?
questions.e: The euro existed on paper from 1999; the cash came three years later.

questions.q: How many pence were in a pre-decimal British shilling?
questions.e: 240 was pence in a pound. Old money was a maths test.

questions.q: Ngarrindjeri inventor and writer David Unaipon appears on which Australian banknote?
questions.e: He patented an improved shearing handpiece in 1909. Edith Cowan, the first woman elected to an Australian parliament, is on the other side.

questions.q: What pseudonym does Bitcoin’s mysterious creator use?
questions.e: Vitalik made Ethereum. Satoshi’s true identity remains unknown.

questions.q: At the Wife Carrying World Championships, the winner traditionally receives?
questions.e: The event is held in Sonkajärvi, Finland. The ‘wife’ doesn’t have to be your wife.

questions.q: In the Cooper’s Hill race in Gloucestershire, England, competitors chase?
questions.e: The cheese can reach about 110 km/h. Nobody catches it. Somebody always breaks something.

questions.q: Chessboxing alternates rounds of chess with rounds of?
questions.e: You can win by checkmate or knockout. Both are equally final.

questions.q: Sepak takraw, popular in Southeast Asia, is like volleyball but players mostly use their?
questions.e: Overhead bicycle-kick spikes are standard. Hands are banned.

questions.q: Quidditch, played by real people with brooms between their legs, was renamed in 2022 to?
questions.e: Partly to distance the sport from the books’ author, partly for trademark reasons.

questions.q: Underwater hockey is also known as?
questions.e: Players push a puck along the bottom of a pool with short sticks, while holding their breath.

questions.q: Hurling, often called the fastest game on grass, is mainly played in?
questions.e: Players use a wooden stick called a hurley to hit a small ball, the sliotar, at well over 100 km/h. It’s over 3,000 years old.

questions.q: Bossaball, invented in Spain, combines volleyball and football with?
questions.e: Played to a soundtrack of samba music. Possibly the most fun sport ever invented.

questions.q: In extreme ironing, people iron clothes?
w: As fast as possible in a relay
questions.e: Started in England in 1997. It’s been done on cliff faces, in canoes and under ice.

questions.q: The Palio di Siena in Italy is a famously chaotic race of?
questions.a: Bareback horses around a town square
questions.e: Held twice each summer in the Piazza del Campo. A horse can win without its rider.

questions.q: What is zero factorial (0!)?
questions.e: There’s exactly one way to arrange nothing. Mathematicians find this hilarious.

questions.q: A googol is 1 followed by how many zeros?
questions.e: Google’s name came from a misspelling of it. Spelling is hard.

questions.q: How many is a baker’s dozen?
questions.e: Bakers threw in an extra to avoid being fined for short loaves.

questions.q: A well-shuffled deck of 52 cards is almost certainly?
questions.a: In an order never seen before
w: Impossible to shuffle twice the same
questions.e: There are more possible orders than atoms on Earth. Your shuffle is unique.

questions.q: How many people need to be in a room for a better than even chance two share a birthday?
questions.e: The birthday paradox. Your intuition is wrong, and that’s fine.
Counts up to 9 and back down. Maths showing off.

questions.q: Which number, written in English, has its letters in alphabetical order?
questions.e: F-O-R-T-Y. The only one. Check if you don’t believe it.

questions.q: Which number did the Roman numeral system have no symbol for?
questions.e: Romans just didn’t write nothing. Reasonable.

questions.q: What is pi rounded to three decimal places?
questions.e: 3.14159... rounds up to 3.142. Truncating is cheating.

questions.q: Before his 1962 orbit, astronaut John Glenn asked for which NASA mathematician to check the computer’s numbers by hand?
questions.e: ‘If she says they’re good, then I’m ready to go.’ Her story is told in Hidden Figures.

questions.q: The claim that hot water can sometimes freeze faster than cold is called the?
questions.e: Named after a Tanzanian schoolboy who noticed it with ice cream. Scientists still argue about it.

questions.q: Old church windows thicker at the bottom are proof that glass?
questions.e: Glass is an amorphous solid. The ‘slow liquid’ story is a myth.

questions.q: Thanks to gravity, clocks tick very slightly faster?
questions.e: Less gravity, faster time. Einstein, being weird again.

questions.q: Sound can’t travel through?
questions.e: In space, no one can hear you. That’s physics, not just a tagline.

questions.q: Which colour of visible light has the longest wavelength?
questions.e: Violet has the shortest. Red is the laid-back one.

questions.q: In 1967, PhD student Jocelyn Bell Burnell spotted a strange, regular blip in her data. It was the first?
questions.e: Her supervisor shared the 1974 Nobel Prize; she didn’t. In 2018 she gave away a $3 million prize to fund physics students from under-represented groups.

questions.q: The half-life of carbon-14 is about?
questions.e: Which is why carbon dating gives up after about 50,000 years.

questions.q: In which year did CERN announce the discovery of the Higgs boson?
questions.e: 2008 was when the Large Hadron Collider switched on. The particle took longer.

questions.q: Absolute zero is about how many degrees Celsius?
questions.e: −459.67 is Fahrenheit. Same zero, worse units.

questions.q: Light from the Sun is white, but the sky is blue because?
questions.e: The ocean reflects the sky, not the other way round.

questions.q: Today is St Andrew’s Day. Andrew is patron saint of?
questions.e: Ireland has Patrick, Wales David, England George. Andrew gets the haggis.

questions.q: Edinburgh Castle sits on top of?
questions.e: Castle Rock. The city is built on old lava. Very metal.

questions.q: What is Scotland’s national animal?
questions.e: Yes, really. A mythical beast for a mythically stubborn nation.

questions.q: Glasgow’s statue of the Duke of Wellington is famous for usually wearing?
questions.e: Locals keep putting it back. It’s practically official now.

questions.q: What is the Loch Ness Monster’s nickname?
questions.e: Sightings remain unconfirmed. Tourism remains excellent.

questions.q: Haggis is traditionally cooked in a sheep’s?
questions.e: Delicious if you don’t think about it.

questions.q: What is Scotland’s national flower?
questions.e: The rose is England’s, the shamrock Ireland’s. The thistle is suitably prickly.

questions.q: What is the highest mountain in the UK?
questions.e: 1345 metres. Snowdon is only Wales’s highest.

questions.q: Who wrote the words of ‘Auld Lang Syne’?
questions.e: Sung every New Year by people who know only the first verse.

questions.q: Which Scottish town is known as the ‘Home of Golf’?
questions.e: Golf’s been played there since the 1400s. Fittingly, it shares today’s saint’s name.
